title: Behaviour of confined masonry wall under cyclic load

title: Seismic Strengthening
text: How can existing masonry-infilled structures be strengthened against seismic demand without adding unnecessary weight or complexity? Doctoral research investigated the confinement of masonry infills in RC moment-resisting frames using cost-effective skin reinforcement, supported by experimental, analytical and numerical studies. In much of South India, framed buildings are filled with unreinforced masonry. The frame is designed; the infill is not. Under cyclic loading the infill attracts force it was never detailed to carry, and can fail out-of-plane even where the frame survives. Panels were tested under cyclic load with skin reinforcement — wire mesh applied to the wall face and anchored into the frame — and compared against unreinforced and confined alternatives. Results were then generalised analytically into an equivalent-strut width that designers can use, and checked numerically. A strengthening method that uses commonly available mesh and mortar, adds little mass, and can be applied to a building that already exists; plus an equivalent-strut formulation for wire-meshed infill under dynamic loading.

title: Masonry Structures
text: What does masonry actually do inside a concrete frame, and how should that be represented in design? Experimental and analytical study of confined masonry, infill–frame interaction, latex-modified and conventional mortars, and alternate wall materials under cyclic load. Masonry is usually treated as non-structural, then behaves structurally. Its stiffness changes how the whole frame responds. Wall panels and portal frames tested under cyclic loading, with variations in mortar, confinement and reinforcement; strut-based idealisations fitted to the measured behaviour. Measured performance for several practical wall build-ups, including latex-modified mortar and natural-fibre brick, and strut-width estimates for meshed infill.

title: 3D Concrete Printing
text: Concrete can now be printed rather than cast — but printed concrete still has to be reinforced. How do you do both at once? Work on printable cementitious mixes, structural build-up and set control, and on print-head and multi-arm systems that integrate reinforcement during deposition. Extrusion printing asks contradictory things of a mix: it must pump and flow, then immediately hold its own shape under the next layer. Separately, reinforcement — the thing that makes concrete structural — is still usually placed by hand, which gives back the time automation saved. On the material side, nano-silica and accelerator systems were studied as structural build-up agents, and alkaline-activated compositions developed for extrusion. On the machine side, a print head for reinforced elements and the TriFusion multi-arm system were developed and filed. Two published patent applications on the material and the print head, a filed system-level application, and a funded prototype currently being built under the Karunya Short-Term Research Grant.

title: Additive Manufacturing in Construction
text: What changes when a building component is manufactured additively instead of formed in a mould? Review and experimental work on additive manufacturing techniques in construction, printable material behaviour and reinforcement integration. Additive methods are mature in other industries and still immature in construction, where scale, ambient conditions and structural codes all differ. A review of the available techniques and their constraints, followed by doctoral supervision and funded prototype work on printable materials and multi-arm deposition. A reviewed account of the technique landscape, a completed doctorate in printable cementitious materials, and filed intellectual property.

title: AI and Machine Learning in Construction
text: Construction generates a great deal of data — images of cracks, fabrication records, material consumption. Can that data be used to predict and to inspect? Deep-learning crack characterisation in buildings; probabilistic grouping and random-forest regression for consumables forecasting in pre-engineered building fabrication. Inspection is manual and inconsistent; fabrication planning relies on estimates that are hard to hold to. Convolutional models trained to characterise cracks from building imagery; regression and grouping models applied to real pre-engineered-building fabrication records. Published methods for both, with a doctoral scholar currently working on classification and forecasting of fabrication dynamics in pre-engineered buildings.

title: BIM and Scan-to-BIM
text: Most existing buildings have no usable digital model. Can one be built from a scan of the building as it actually stands? Techniques, mapping strategies and building life-cycle applications for integrating scan data into BIM. Drawings, where they exist, record what was intended rather than what was built. Assessment and retrofit both need the second. A structured review of capture techniques and of the mapping strategies that turn point-cloud data into structured model elements, organised by life-cycle stage. A consolidated account of where scan-to-BIM currently works and where it does not.

title: Structural Health Monitoring
text: How do we know whether a structure is still sound, without taking it apart? Damage characterisation from building imagery and scan data, alongside damping and response studies on framed structures. Condition assessment is periodic, subjective and often too late. Imaging and deep learning for crack characterisation; scan-derived models as a geometric baseline; experimental work on damping devices and structural response. Published crack-characterisation methods and a body of measured response data for damped frames.

title: Structural Engineering
text: How do framed structures carry load, and how can their response be controlled? Composite and encased frames under cyclic load, buckling-restrained braces, fluid-viscous and magnetorheological dampers, topology optimisation, and code-comparison studies. Controlling the response of a frame — rather than only sizing it — is what determines how it performs in an earthquake or a wind event. Experimental cyclic testing of composite and steel-encased frames, and analytical and numerical study of bracing, damping devices and optimisation methods. A sustained experimental record on composite frames and damping systems, including comparative work at two damper scales.

title: Construction Materials
text: Can a material be made to perform better, cost less, or use less of what is scarce? Toughness enhancement in cement mortar, latex-modified mortar, self-compacting concrete with copper slag and fly ash, sea sand as partial replacement for M-sand, natural-fibre brick, metakaolin-blended blocks and soil stabilisation. River sand and clinker are both constrained; performance requirements are not. Systematic mix-level experimental programmes, each substituting one constituent and measuring the consequence. A long series of characterised alternatives, several of which feed directly into the printable-material and masonry work.

title: Sustainable Construction
text: Can construction use waste streams and lower-clinker binders without giving up structural performance? Industrial by-products as aggregate and binder replacement, alkaline-activated compositions, bamboo reinforcement and agricultural-waste-based blocks. Cement production and sand extraction both carry costs that the structure itself never records. Replacement studies across concrete and masonry, evaluated on strength and workability rather than on intent. Measured performance for copper slag, fly ash, metakaolin-blended palm kernel shell, sea sand and bamboo in specific applications.

title: Mixed Reality in Construction
text: Can a model be read on site, against the structure itself, rather than on a drawing? An active research interest in mixed-reality methods for construction, developing alongside the scan-to-BIM work. The gap between a digital model and the site is still crossed by paper. Currently a direction of inquiry rather than a completed programme; it follows naturally from the scan-to-BIM results.

title: Environment and Health
text: What is in the air, and what does it do to the people breathing it? Collaborative work on bioaerosol characterisation and sampling, rural airborne microorganisms and antimicrobial resistance, and climatic determinants of public-health incidence. Air quality and the built environment are not separate problems, but they are usually studied separately. Co-authored interdisciplinary studies with environmental science and public-health colleagues. Contributing author on several studies, including a widely cited review of bioaerosol characterisation and sampling.

title: GI Nettings for Partially Restrained RCC Beam–Column Joint
text: A reinforcement approach using characterised GI wire netting at RCC beam–column joints, developed to address reinforcement congestion and improve seismic performance. Beam–column joints carry the highest concentration of reinforcement in a moment-resisting frame, and that congestion makes them difficult to detail and to cast well. This method introduces characterised galvanised-iron netting at the joint as a partial restraint, reducing the shear reinforcement needed in the confined region while maintaining joint performance under cyclic demand. E. Arunraj S. Vincent Sam Jebadurai G. Hemalatha 389408 202041037408

title: 3D Printing Head for Reinforced Concrete Structural Elements
text: A print-head arrangement for depositing reinforced concrete structural elements, addressing the central difficulty of combining extrusion with reinforcement. Conventional concrete 3D printing deposits material in layers but leaves reinforcement as a separate, largely manual operation. This application covers a print head intended to bring the two together at the point of deposition for structural elements. Pratheeksh Joshy Sajin Philip S. Vincent Sam Jebadurai G. Hemalatha 202341009604

title: An Alkaline-Activated Cementitious Material-Based Mixture Composition for an Extrudable Type 3D Printer
text: A mixture composition using alkaline-activated cementitious material, formulated for extrusion-based construction 3D printing. Extrusion printing constrains a mix from both directions: it must flow through the nozzle and then hold its own shape immediately afterwards. This composition approaches that window using alkaline activation rather than ordinary Portland cement alone, which also lowers the clinker content of the printed material. Sheeja T. V. S. Vincent Sam Jebadurai G. Hemalatha 202441008317

title: TriFusion 3D Automated Building Construction System
text: An automated building-construction system combining multiple print arms so that deposition and reinforcement placement can proceed together. TriFusion is the system-level counterpart to the print-head work: rather than treating printing, reinforcement and finishing as sequential operations, it coordinates them across multiple arms. It is the invention behind the multi-arm printing project currently funded under the Karunya Short-Term Research Grant. S. Vincent Sam Jebadurai L. Godson Asirvatham Bairi Levi Rakshith

title: Development of Multi-arm 3D Printing System with Integrated Horizontal and Vertical Reinforcement
text: Concrete 3D printing can place material accurately, but reinforcement still largely has to be added by hand, which removes much of the advantage automation offers. This project develops a multi-arm printing system in which horizontal and vertical reinforcement is integrated during deposition rather than afterwards. Karunya Short-Term Research Grant (KSRG) — Seed Money Principal Investigator
